systems-001.question: Which frequency band is typically refracted and reflected by the ionosphere so that it can reach far beyond the line of sight, sometimes to the other side of the earth?
choices: SHF (super high frequency, centimeter waves, 3–30 GHz)
systems-001.explanation: HF (3–30 MHz) waves are refracted by ionospheric layers such as the F layer and return to the ground; by bouncing repeatedly between the ground and the ionosphere they can reach long distances. That is why shortwave has been used for international broadcasting, amateur radio, and long-distance communication with ships and aircraft. The highest frequency that returns is set by the electron density of the ionosphere and changes with time of day, season and solar activity. UHF and SHF waves normally pass straight through the ionosphere, so on the ground they are used mainly for line-of-sight communication, and that same property makes them suitable for communicating with satellites.

systems-002.question: In the ITU frequency band designations, which band does a 1.5 GHz radio wave fall in?
choices: SHF (super high frequency, centimeter waves, 3–30 GHz)
systems-002.explanation: The ITU designations divide frequency into decades: VHF is 30–300 MHz, UHF is 300 MHz–3 GHz, SHF is 3–30 GHz, and EHF is 30–300 GHz. 1.5 GHz falls in UHF, with a wavelength of 20 cm. In terms of wavelength, VHF corresponds to 1–10 m (metric waves), UHF to 10 cm–1 m (decimetric waves), and SHF to 1–10 cm (centimetric waves). VHF is used for FM broadcasting and similar services, SHF for satellite broadcasting and 5 GHz wireless LAN, and UHF for cellular phones, GNSS and digital terrestrial television.

systems-003.question: In the IEEE radar frequency band designations (names such as L band and S band), which band contains 10 GHz?
systems-003.explanation: In the IEEE designations, L band is 1–2 GHz, S band 2–4 GHz, C band 4–8 GHz, X band 8–12 GHz, Ku band 12–18 GHz, K band 18–27 GHz, and Ka band 27–40 GHz (the K/Ka boundary is sometimes taken as 26.5 GHz, and in satellite communications the downlink around 20 GHz is conventionally also called Ka band). 10 GHz is in X band; its short 3 cm wavelength gives sharp beams from small antennas, so it is widely used for marine and weather radar. C band is relatively little affected by rain and has long been used for satellite communications, and Ku band is used for satellite broadcasting and similar services.

systems-004.question: What is the wavelength in vacuum of a 60 GHz radio wave? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
systems-004.explanation: λ = c/f = 3×10⁸/(60×10⁹) = 5×10⁻³ m = 5 mm. Frequencies of 30–300 GHz have wavelengths of 1–10 mm and are called millimeter waves (EHF). 50 mm is the wavelength at 6 GHz and 0.5 mm at 600 GHz, the result of mishandling the GHz order of magnitude. Because the wavelength is short, antennas of a given gain can be very small, and array antennas with many elements can be built in a few centimeters square. On the other hand, compared with fixed-gain antennas the free-space path loss rises with the square of frequency, and at 60 GHz oxygen absorption is added, so the band suits short-range communication.

systems-005.question: In clear weather, what is the main cause of the particularly large atmospheric attenuation around 60 GHz?
systems-005.explanation: Oxygen molecules in the atmosphere have many absorption lines around 60 GHz, producing a large attenuation of roughly 15 dB/km near the ground. This makes the 60 GHz band unsuitable for long-distance links, but its short reach is exploited for high-speed short-range communication. Water vapor absorption peaks are around 22 GHz and 183 GHz, and are not the main cause of attenuation near 60 GHz. The ionosphere affects much lower frequencies such as HF; millimeter waves pass through it.

systems-006.question: In satellite communications, which of the following links is most affected by rain attenuation (for the same rain intensity)?
choices: C band (uplink about 6 GHz, downlink about 4 GHz)
Ka band (uplink about 30 GHz, downlink about 20 GHz)
L band (uplink about 1.6 GHz, downlink about 1.5 GHz)
systems-006.explanation: As the wavelength approaches the size of raindrops (a few millimeters), the waves are more easily absorbed and scattered by them, so rain attenuation increases sharply with frequency. In the satellite Ka band (uplink about 30 GHz, downlink about 20 GHz; the IEEE Ka band is 27–40 GHz, but in satellite communications the 20 GHz downlink is conventionally included), heavy rain can cause attenuation of several tens of dB, so link designs need countermeasures such as large rain margins or temporarily raising transmit power. C band is little affected by rain, so it has been used for satellite links even in rainy regions. In L band, rain attenuation is hardly an issue.

systems-007.question: A transmitter outputs 10 W (+40 dBm), the feed line to the antenna has 2 dB of loss, and the antenna gain is 15 dBi. What is the EIRP (equivalent isotropically radiated power)?
systems-007.explanation: EIRP converts the power an antenna radiates in its direction of maximum radiation into the power an isotropic antenna would need to produce the same power density: EIRP = transmitter output − feed line loss + antenna gain = 40 − 2 + 15 = +53 dBm (about 200 W, or 23 dBW). +57 dBm adds the feed line loss, and +27 dBm reverses the signs of both the gain and the loss. Because it represents the strength actually emitted in that direction, including antenna gain, rather than the transmitter output itself, EIRP is widely used in link design and in regulations on transmit strength.

systems-008.question: A link has an EIRP of +30 dBm, a propagation loss of 120 dB, a receive antenna gain of 10 dBi, a receive-side feed line loss of 1 dB, and a receiver sensitivity of −90 dBm. What is the link margin?
systems-008.explanation: The received power is Pr = EIRP − propagation loss + receive antenna gain − feed line loss = 30 − 120 + 10 − 1 = −81 dBm. The link margin is the difference between received power and sensitivity: −81 − (−90) = 9 dB. 11 dB adds the feed line loss, and −1 dB is the value when the receive antenna gain is left out. On real links, fading, rain, obstacles and component variation lower the received power, so transmit power and antennas are chosen to secure a margin that covers them.

systems-009.question: On a free-space line-of-sight link, the receiver sensitivity is improved by 6 dB (so weaker signals can be received). With all else the same, by roughly what factor does the maximum communication distance increase?
systems-009.explanation: In free space the received power is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, so if the minimum receivable power drops to 1/4 (−6 dB), the distance can be extended by √4 = 2 times. About 4 times wrongly assumes the received power is inversely proportional to distance. About 1.4 times (the fourth root of 4) applies when the received power falls with the fourth power of distance (as at long range in the two-ray model including ground reflection), not in free space. Sensitivity can be improved by lowering the noise figure, narrowing the bandwidth, or using modulation and error correction that need a lower SNR.

systems-010.question: In transmitter evaluation, which is the correct main cause of a degraded adjacent channel leakage ratio (ACLR)?
choices: Intermodulation distortion from power amplifier nonlinearity spreads the signal spectrum into the neighboring channel
The transmit antenna gain is too high, so the waves reach neighboring areas that use the adjacent channel
The receiver's noise figure is high, so the noise in both its own channel and the neighboring channel increases, narrowing the power ratio between them
systems-010.explanation: ACLR is the ratio of the transmit power in one's own channel to the power leaking into the adjacent channel, and it expresses how much interference the transmitter causes to other users. A wideband modulated signal has many frequency components, and when third-order and other nonlinearities in the amplifier cause intermodulation among them, shoulders of spectrum spread outside the original band. This is called spectral regrowth. Distortion rises sharply as output is raised, so it is suppressed with backoff or digital predistortion (DPD). Antenna gain concerns spatial spread, not spillover in frequency. Noise figure is a receiver property and has nothing to do with transmit ACLR.

systems-011.question: Which is closest to the altitude above the earth's surface of a geostationary satellite over the equator?
systems-011.explanation: A geostationary satellite is in an orbit above the equator with the same period as the earth's rotation (about 23 hours 56 minutes), at an altitude of about 35,786 km, roughly 36,000 km. From the ground it appears fixed at the same point in the sky, so communication and broadcasting can be done with fixed antennas. About 20,000 km is the altitude of medium-earth-orbit satellites such as GPS, and about 400 km is a low earth orbit like that of the International Space Station. Because of their high altitude, three geostationary satellites can cover almost the whole world (except the polar regions), but propagation loss and delay are large.

systems-012.question: Which is closest to the time for a radio wave to travel from ground station A to ground station B via a geostationary satellite? Take the distance to the satellite as 36,000 km for both stations and the speed of light as 3×10⁵ km/s.
systems-012.explanation: The total distance from station A to the satellite and from the satellite to station B is 2 × 36,000 = 72,000 km. Dividing by the speed of light, 3×10⁵ km/s, gives 72,000/300,000 = 0.24 s. About 0.12 s is the time for only the uplink or the downlink. About 0.48 s corresponds to the round trip for B to respond to a signal from A and for the response to return to A. This delay is noticeable in telephone conversations, and it also limits throughput in protocols that wait for acknowledgments while sending. In practice, the farther a station is from the point directly beneath the satellite, the longer the distance to the satellite and the slightly larger the delay.

systems-013.question: Which is closest to the free-space path loss at 12 GHz from a geostationary satellite 36,000 km away? Use L = 32.45 + 20 log₁₀ f(MHz) + 20 log₁₀ d(km) dB, with log₁₀ 1.2 ≈ 0.079 and log₁₀ 3.6 ≈ 0.556.
systems-013.explanation: 20 log₁₀ 12000 = 20 × (4 + 0.079) ≈ 81.6 dB and 20 log₁₀ 36000 = 20 × (4 + 0.556) ≈ 91.1 dB, so L ≈ 32.45 + 81.6 + 91.1 ≈ 205.2 dB. About 145 dB plugs in the frequency in GHz (12); this form of the formula takes MHz and km. About 265 dB enters the distance in meters (60 dB too much). To overcome a loss of around 200 dB, satellite broadcast reception uses high-gain parabolic antennas and low-noise converters.

systems-014.question: With an antenna noise temperature of 50 K and an equivalent noise temperature of 150 K for the receiver connected directly to the antenna, what is the system noise temperature of the receiving system (referred to the antenna terminals)?
systems-014.explanation: Noise temperature is proportional to noise power, so the contributions of independent noise sources add. The 50 K of noise the antenna picks up from the sky and ground (the antenna noise temperature) plus the 150 K of the receiver's own noise referred to its input give a system noise temperature Tsys = 50 + 150 = 200 K. 100 K takes the average; noise adds up rather than averaging. 150 K considers only the receiver. For a satellite receiving antenna pointed at the sky, the antenna noise temperature is far below the terrestrial 290 K, so a low receiver noise temperature has a large effect on performance. Any loss between the antenna and the receiver adds its noise as well.

systems-015.question: A receiving station has an antenna gain of 40 dBi and a system noise temperature of 200 K. What is its figure of merit G/T (take 10 log₁₀ 200 ≈ 23 dB)?
systems-015.explanation: G/T is the receive antenna gain divided by the system noise temperature; in dB it is G − 10 log₁₀ T = 40 − 23 = 17 dB/K. The received power is proportional to gain, and the noise power kTB is proportional to noise temperature, so the larger the G/T, the higher the received C/N0; it expresses the performance of a receiving station in a single number. In link calculations it is used as C/N0 = EIRP − propagation loss + G/T + 228.6 dB (228.6 is −10 log₁₀ k for Boltzmann's constant). About 63 dB/K adds instead of subtracting, and about −17 dB/K inverts the ratio to T/G. G/T improves with a larger antenna or a lower receiver noise temperature.
